thesis: This episode primarily uses Trader Joe's as a case study to contrast its unique business model against larger competitors like Costco, Amazon, and Kroger, highlighting differences in scale, SKU strategy, and valuation multiples. It also briefly touches on the 'American holy trinity' of essential companies, though specific investment views on those broader categories are not the central argument.

claims.claim: The speakers note a connection between Trader Joe's and Nvidia because Jensen Huang was a coworker of Trader Joe's founders.
claims.quote: David: Yes, me too. But there is a direct connection between Trader Joe's and Nvidia via coworkers. Ben: You heard it here first. Trader Joe and Jensen Huang were coworkers at one point in time.

claims.claim: Ben praises Apple products, specifically AirPods, calling them awesome, great, and noting that Apple gets better iteratively.
claims.quote: Ben: Let's do it, because I can't help myself: ordering every Apple product and most new tech gadgets that come out and then just having a giant pile of them. I ordered AirPods 3 on launch day with my new phone, and they're awesome. It's just crazy how Apple gets better and better iteratively each time with these things.

claims.claim: David states a preference for Meta glasses over AirPods, noting he doesn't like having things in his ears.
claims.quote: David: I can second that. I got them, too. By far the best AirPods yet. I still prefer the Meta glasses, though. I've just realized I really don't like having things in my ears.

claims.claim: Ben suggests an episode on Amazon Part 1 may be of interest because Trader Joe's is described as the anti-Amazon.
claims.quote: Ben: Absolutely. Walmart. Perhaps Amazon Part 1 also may be of interest, since this is effectively the anti-Amazon: it's the everything store and the very few things store.

claims.claim: David mentions that they made an episode on Whole Foods back in the day, specifically the day Amazon bought the company.
claims.quote: David: Oh, and Ben, how could we forget? We made an episode on Whole Foods back in the day. Ben: We did. David: The day that Amazon bought the company.

claims.claim: Costco is described as the 'jewel of the industry' with high growth and margins, trading at a high multiple.
claims.quote: Costco is growing about 8% per year, so probably a little slower than Trader Joe's by most estimates, and has a 3% net income margin. Costco trades at 1.6x revenue, sky high.

claims.claim: Walmart is used as a second comparison point, having similar margins and growth to Costco but trading at a lower multiple.
claims.quote: Walmart, which isn't all grocery, but a lot of it is grocery, has similar net income margins, similar growth. Maybe it grows a little slower than Costco. Walmart trades at 1.3x revenue.

claims.claim: Kroger is described as a slower growth business with shrinking revenue and razor-thin net income margins.
claims.quote: Kroger trades at 0.3x revenue and Albertsons at 0.1x revenue. Those are much slower growth businesses. And Kroger is actually shrinking with razor-thin net income margins between 1 and 2%.

claims.claim: Kroger is mentioned in a question about its valuation multiple compared to other retailers.
claims.quote: Okay, what does Kroger trade at?

claims.claim: Lockheed Martin is referenced as a previous episode example where a company is essential but not super valuable by typical standards.
claims.quote: It's almost like the Lockheed Martin episode that we did. It's not a super valuable company by the standards of what we typically cover on Acquired. It is one of the most important companies in the world.

claims.claim: Amazon is mentioned as a company that would fail if it tried to operate with a low SKU count like Trader Joe's.
claims.quote: It works with their brand promise in a way that Walmart Mini would totally fail. A Walmart with less stuff? I'm not going there. The whole premise of Walmart is all the stuff.

claims.claim: Costco is a much bigger business than Trader Joe's with revenue 10x larger, though margins are lower at 11-14%.
claims.quote: By the way, we should say for anyone who's wondering, Costco is a much, much, much bigger business than Trader Joe's. They're sort of cousins of each other in business model, different in all the ways we've talked about. But Costco's revenue is 10x—maybe more.

claims.claim: Costco's revenue last year was $275 billion.
claims.quote: Last year, it was $275 billion.

claims.claim: Costco is an international business.
claims.quote: David: Yep. And to my point about international, Costco is an international business.

claims.claim: Costco is a successful public company doing great.
claims.quote: David: And they're obviously doing great as a successful public company.
